mcq.q: You switch embedding models with the same dimensions. You must…
options: Do nothing, since the dimensions of both models match
Re-embed the corpus; switch query encoder and index together
Only re-embed the documents that are added from now on
Normalise the old vectors so they fit the new model's scale
mcq.why: Different models produce incompatible vector spaces even at equal dimensions.
distractors: Matching dimensions do not make the spaces compatible.
Old and new vectors would be in different spaces.
Normalising does not change which space they are in.

mcq.q: A team switched its query encoder to model B to improve search, but left the documents embedded with model A. Results became nonsense. Why?
options: They use different databases
They have different lengths only
Model B is always better
They live in different vector spaces
mcq.why: Scores can look normal while results are random.
distractors: Even equal dimensions do not make them compatible.

mcq.q: Why should queries reach an index through an alias such as kb-search?
options: So switching indexes is one atomic alias change
Aliases reduce the storage that indexes need
Aliases make each query faster to run
Aliases encrypt the data behind the index
mcq.why: Rollback is then switching the alias back.
distractors: Aliases are names; they store nothing.
They are not a security feature.

mcq.q: How is the new index backfilled when only the embedding model changes?
options: By asking users to search so pages get indexed
By copying the old vectors into the new index
From stored chunk text, throttled, without re-parsing
By re-crawling every source system from scratch
mcq.why: Re-parsing is needed only if the chunker or parser changed.
distractors: Old vectors are in the old model's space.
Not needed if the chunker is unchanged.

mcq.q: What does dual-writing during a migration do?
options: Doubles the query traffic to test the new index
Writes every change twice to the same index
Deletes the old index once the new one is ready
Sends each change to both indexes so v4 keeps up
mcq.why: The backfill and live changes both reach v4.
distractors: It writes to two different indexes.

mcq.q: What must happen before cutting over to the new index?
options: Deleting the old index to free space
Nothing; switch and watch metrics
Changing the answer prompt to match
Offline evaluation meeting the gates
mcq.why: Then shadow or canary reads.
distractors: Deleting first removes the rollback path.
The prompt is unrelated to the index.

mcq.q: At cut-over a team switches the alias to v4, but the query service still embeds questions with the old model. What should have switched at the same moment?
options: The vector database vendor
The query-side embedding model
The answer-generating model
The chunk size of the corpus
mcq.why: Otherwise queries are embedded for the wrong space.
distractors: The LLM is unaffected by the index.

mcq.q: Why keep the old index warm after cut-over?
options: To save storage during the cut-over
So rollback is just switching the alias back
To train the new embedding model
For extra speed on busy days
mcq.why: For example, two weeks.

mcq.q: What is the peak extra cost of a blue/green index migration?
options: About half the storage, as old vectors shrink
About double storage during the overlap
About ten times the compute of normal serving
No extra cost, since the indexes share data
mcq.why: Budget for it in capacity plans.
distractors: Both indexes exist during the overlap.
Each index stores its own vectors.

mcq.q: What should an index manifest record?
options: The users who searched the index, with their query counts
Only the number of vectors stored and the date of the last write
Only the index's name, owner team and creation date
Embedding model and version, dimensions, chunker, parser, ANN settings
mcq.why: A query service can refuse an index whose embedder differs from its own.
distractors: Users are not part of the index's identity.
A count does not show compatibility.
A name says nothing about its contents.

mcq.q: Re-embedding 65 million chunks of about 400 tokens each at an illustrative $0.02 per million tokens costs roughly how much?
options: About $52
About $5,200
About $520
About $1.30
mcq.why: 65M × 400 = 26 billion tokens; 26,000 million × $0.02 ≈ $520. Throttling and double storage add to the real bill.
distractors: That drops a factor of ten in the token count.
That adds a factor of ten.

mcq.q: Two days after cutting over to index v4, answer quality drops for one language. v3 was retired at cut-over. What did the migration skip?
options: A larger efSearch on v4, which would have fixed the language
A rollback window with v3 kept warm, so the alias could be switched back
Dual-writing after cut-over, which keeps both indexes current
A bigger answer model to absorb the retrieval change
mcq.why: Keeping the old index warm makes rollback a single alias change.
distractors: Search settings do not restore the old index.
Dual-writing helps only while the old index still exists.
The answer model cannot fix the retrieval regression.

interview.q: Why is changing the embedding model a migration, not a config change?
interview.followUp: What breaks if you skip re-embedding the old documents?

interview.q: Walk through a blue/green index migration.
covers: Switch alias with the query encoder; keep v3 warm
interview.followUp: Which step would you be most tempted to skip, and what is the risk?

interview.q: What is an index manifest, and what does it prevent?
covers: Records model, chunker, parser and ANN settings
interview.followUp: How would the query service use the manifest at startup?

interview.q: You switched embedding models and recall dropped. How do you roll back safely?
interview.followUp: What would you change in the process so this is caught before cut-over?

interview.q: Estimate the cost and duration of re-embedding 65 million chunks.
interview.followUp: How would you keep the backfill from slowing production search?

interview.q: How would you migrate when the chunker changes too?

mcq.q: A stale queued update overwrote a newer document. The fix is…
options: More workers to process the queue faster
A version (compare-and-set) guard on writes
A bigger queue so nothing is dropped
Fewer retries so old jobs give up sooner
mcq.why: Write only if the incoming version is newer than the stored one.
distractors: Faster processing does not stop reordering.
Retry counts do not order writes.

mcq.q: How are incremental updates usually detected?
options: Change feeds, webhooks, CDC or hash diffs
Random sampling of documents each day
Complaints from users about stale answers
Re-indexing everything daily from scratch
mcq.why: Only what changed is processed.

mcq.q: How should a changed document's chunks be replaced?
options: Append the new chunks and keep the old ones
Delete everything first, then rebuild slowly
Atomically: old out, new in, in one step
Edit chunks in place, one at a time
mcq.why: Queries should never see both versions, or neither.
distractors: Readers see a mix of versions.

mcq.q: A source document is deleted. What must also be removed?
options: Its chunks, cached answers and summaries
Only the cached answers that quote it
Only the original file at its source
Nothing, since nobody will search for it
mcq.why: Deletion speed can be a legal requirement (16.5).
distractors: The index would still serve it.
Deleted content can still be retrieved.

mcq.q: Many connectors miss deletes. What catches them?
options: Adding more replicas of the index
Periodic reconciliation against the source
Waiting for users to report stale results
Bigger queues to hold the delete events
mcq.why: Reconciliation repairs what missed events left stale.
distractors: The events are missing, not delayed.

mcq.q: When deduplicating copies of a file across sites, what must you remember?
options: Only the first location it was found in
Nothing, since the content is identical
Only the location of the largest copy
All locations, as permissions may differ
mcq.why: Keep one canonical chunk set, with the permission sets of every copy.
distractors: Other copies may have different permissions.
Each copy may differ in who can see it.

mcq.q: Which fields belong in a chunk's lineage?
options: Only the chunk's text and the date it was last shown
Only the user who searched for it and when they did
Only the chunk's vector and the ANN index it lives in
Source, document ID, version, parser, chunker, embedder, times
mcq.why: Lineage answers “why did the assistant say this?” and “what must be rebuilt?”.
distractors: Vectors do not say where they came from.

mcq.q: How is a freshness guarantee measured?
options: indexed_at − source_modified_at per change
By query latency at p95 during the day
By the total size of the index over time
By the number of documents indexed per hour
mcq.why: For example, 99% of edits searchable within 10 minutes.

mcq.q: Unchanged chunks of an edited document have the same content hash. What can you do?
options: Delete them, since they are duplicates
Re-embed them anyway, to be safe
Move them to a separate index
Reuse their vectors to save cost
mcq.why: Only changed chunks need new vectors.
distractors: That wastes cost on unchanged text.

mcq.q: Five changes had lags of 2, 3, 4, 5 and 30 minutes. The target is 99% within 10 minutes. Is it met?
options: It cannot be measured from five changes
No: only 80% were within 10 minutes
Yes, the average is 8.8 minutes
Yes
mcq.why: Freshness is a percentile target, not an average.
distractors: It can; five changes are a small sample.
The average hides the 30-minute change; only 4 of 5 met the target.

mcq.q: An employee leaves, and their shared drive is deleted. A week later the assistant still quotes a file from it. The connector sends edits but no delete events. What should have caught it?
options: Deduplicating the file against other copies of it
Re-embedding the file with the newest embedding model
A shorter freshness SLO for edits, measured per change
Periodic reconciliation: list source IDs and remove what is gone
mcq.why: Many connectors miss deletes; diffing the source against the index catches them.
distractors: Deduplication does not remove deleted sources.
The file should be removed, not re-embedded.
Edits were fine; deletes were never sent.

mcq.q: An edited document had 40 chunks; 34 are unchanged by content hash. Embedding costs 0.5 cents per chunk. What does reusing the unchanged vectors save on this edit?
options: 17 cents: only 6 chunks need new embeddings
20 cents, the cost of the whole document
Nothing, since vectors cannot be reused
3 cents, the cost of the 6 changed chunks
mcq.why: 34 unchanged × 0.5¢ = 17¢ saved; 6 × 0.5¢ = 3¢ is still spent.
distractors: The 6 changed chunks still need embedding.
Same hash, same text, same vector.
That is what is still spent, not what is saved.

mcq.q: One tenant has 70% of traffic and lives on one shard. Best mitigation?
options: More replicas for every shard in the cluster
Dedicated shards and replicas for that tenant
A larger HNSW M on that tenant's shard
A higher efSearch for that tenant's queries
mcq.why: Isolate and scale the hot tenant's own capacity.
distractors: Extra replicas everywhere spread capacity that the hot tenant cannot use.
Graph connectivity does not add capacity for one shard.
A higher efSearch makes each query slower, adding load.

mcq.q: What is the difference between a shard and a replica?
options: A shard is a subset; a replica is a copy of a shard
A replica is a subset; a shard is a full copy
A shard is a cache in front of the index
They are the same thing under two names
mcq.why: Shards scale data and writes; replicas scale reads and availability.
distractors: One splits data; the other copies it.

mcq.q: What is scatter-gather?
options: Copying data out to the replicas
Deleting old shards after a move
Caching results for repeated queries
Fanning out to shards and merging results
mcq.why: Hash placement makes every query touch every shard.

mcq.q: What is the trade-off of placing documents by tenant?
options: It needs no metadata on documents, only their text
Every query hits every shard, whatever its tenant
It gives no isolation between tenants at all
Few shards per query, good isolation, uneven sizes
mcq.why: Hash placement spreads load evenly but fans out every query.

mcq.q: What is a hot tenant?
options: A tenant served from a cache
One tenant overloading its shard
A deleted tenant's leftover data
A tenant with no data at all
mcq.why: A noisy neighbour (15.5).
distractors: That would be cold, not hot.

mcq.q: How much memory headroom does the topic suggest for index rebuilds?
options: None; plan for exactly the data
Typically 30–50%
About 5% on top of the data
About 200% on top of the data
mcq.why: Rebuilds and growth need space.

mcq.q: Ingestion is the bottleneck. A team adds replicas. What happens?
options: Little: replicas help reads, not writes
Ingestion speeds up a lot right away
It reduces the storage the index uses
Write latency halves for each replica
mcq.why: Writes go to every replica, so replicas can even add write work.
distractors: Writes still go to every replica.

mcq.q: When should a shard be split?
options: Never; shards grow without limit
When it is empty and unused
Before a node can no longer rebuild it fast
Only after an outage shows the need
mcq.why: Long rebuilds extend the time at reduced redundancy.

mcq.q: A platform has 12,000 tenants and gives the 50 largest dedicated collections. How many share the common shards?
In the mixed strategy, when is a tenant promoted to dedicated shards?
options: When it complains about speed
Past about 5M chunks or 50 QPS
When it first signs up
Never; all tenants share shards
mcq.why: Thresholds based on size and traffic.
distractors: Promotion is by measured size and load.

mcq.q: An index has 120 GB of vectors, graph links and metadata. It runs with 2 replicas in total and needs 40% rebuild headroom. Roughly how much memory should you plan?
options: About 336 GB
About 240 GB
About 168 GB
About 288 GB
mcq.why: 120 × 2 = 240 GB, plus 40% headroom = 336 GB.
distractors: That adds headroom to one copy only.

mcq.q: Hash placement spreads a SaaS index evenly over 16 shards, but small tenants complain that every query is slow. Why, and what helps?
options: The shards are uneven in size; switch to hashing by chunk ID
efSearch is too low; raise it so queries finish faster
Every query fans out to all 16 shards; place small tenants by tenant
Replicas are missing; add replicas to every shard at once
mcq.why: Hashing evens the load but makes each query touch every shard. Tenant placement keeps a small tenant's queries on one shard.
distractors: The index already uses hashing, which keeps shards even.
A higher efSearch makes each query slower.
Replicas add read capacity, not fewer fan-outs.

interview.followUp: What would make you switch strategy later?

mcq.q: 10 million documents × 6 pages × 500 tokens per page is how many tokens?
options: 3 billion
30 billion
300 billion
30 million
distractors: Three orders of magnitude too few.

mcq.q: 30 billion tokens in 512-token chunks with 10% overlap gives about how many chunks?
options: About 65 million
About 650 million
About 59 million
About 6.5 million
mcq.why: Each chunk adds about 461 new tokens: 3 × 10¹⁰ ÷ 461 ≈ 65 million.

mcq.q: 65 million 768-dimension float32 vectors take about how much space?
options: About 50 GB
About 20 GB
About 2 TB
About 200 GB

mcq.q: The same vectors in int8 take about how much?
options: About 100 GB
About 6 GB
About 200 GB
About 50 GB
mcq.why: int8 is a quarter of float32.

mcq.q: HNSW links at about 128 bytes per vector add how much for 65 million vectors?
options: About 8 GB
About 128 GB
About 0.8 GB
About 80 GB
distractors: That confuses bytes per vector with GB.

mcq.q: int8 vectors (50 GB) plus links (8 GB), with 2 replicas, need about how much RAM across the cluster?
options: About 58 GB
About 400 GB
About 16 GB
About 116 GB
mcq.why: (50 + 8) × 2 = 116 GB, before metadata and rebuild headroom.

mcq.q: Embedding about 33 billion chunk tokens once at an illustrative $0.02 per million tokens costs about…
mcq.why: 3.3 × 10⁴ million tokens × $0.02 ≈ $660–670, repeated on every embedding-model change.

mcq.q: Why measure sizing assumptions on a sample of your real corpus?
options: Samples cost nothing to collect and measure
Each assumption changes the result several-fold
Calculators are always exact for any corpus
Vendors require a sample before quoting
mcq.why: Pages, tokens, chunk size, overlap, dimensions, precision and replicas all multiply.

mcq.q: A plan counts only raw vector bytes as the RAM requirement. What is missing?
options: The answer model's weights in memory
The tokenizer's vocabulary for queries
Graph links, metadata, replicas, headroom
Nothing; raw vectors are the whole index
mcq.why: Total memory is several times the raw vectors.

mcq.q: What repeats the full embedding cost?
options: Adding a replica of the index
Changing the answer prompt
Changing the embedding model
Adding a new user account
mcq.why: Every vector must be recomputed (10.7).

mcq.q: What does a durable queue between ingestion stages provide?
options: Faster embeddings for each chunk processed
Decoupling: each stage scales and fails alone
Smaller vectors stored in the index
Better answers from the language model
mcq.why: Producers and consumers no longer need to run at the same speed.

mcq.q: What is a checkpoint in ingestion?
options: A saved model checkpoint from training
A cache of parsed results for reuse later
A permission check on each document read
A durable progress record, so jobs resume
mcq.why: For example, a connector's last sync cursor.
distractors: A cache is not progress tracking.

mcq.q: What is backpressure?
options: Adding more queues between stages
Retrying failed items faster
Deleting old messages to make room
Slowing upstream when downstream lags
mcq.why: Bounded queues and consumer-paced pulling implement it.
distractors: More queues do not slow producers.

mcq.q: What is a dead-letter queue for?
options: All items that succeeded
Cached answers for reuse
Documents deleted at source
Items past their retry limit
mcq.why: Monitor and replay it.

mcq.q: Why derive chunk IDs from document ID + version + position?
options: To keep the IDs short and readable
So reprocessing gives the same result
To hide which document a chunk is from
To sort chunks alphabetically
mcq.why: At-least-once delivery then produces no duplicates.
distractors: The ID reveals it on purpose.

mcq.q: An old version's job finishes after a newer one. What prevents it from overwriting fresh content?
options: A version guard (compare-and-set) on writes
A larger queue so jobs wait in order
Faster workers so jobs finish sooner
More retries so failed jobs finish later
mcq.why: Queues redeliver and reorder.

mcq.q: When should a worker acknowledge a message?
options: Before parsing begins, to free the queue
As soon as it is received by the worker
Never, so the message is always kept
After the result is durably committed
mcq.why: Early acknowledgement loses work on a crash.
distractors: A crash would lose the item.
The message would be redelivered forever.

mcq.q: 4 workers process 20 documents per second each, and 100 documents arrive per second. How fast does the queue grow?
options: 100 per second
20 per second
80 per second
It shrinks over time
mcq.why: Capacity is 80/s, so 20/s accumulate.
distractors: That ignores the workers' 80 per second.

mcq.q: Worker latency looks fine, but the oldest message in the queue keeps getting older. What is happening?
options: The queue is empty and the system idle
A freshness incident: work is backing up
Everything is healthy, as latency shows
The workers are sitting idle and waiting
mcq.why: Watch queue age, not just worker speed.
distractors: They are busy but too few.

mcq.q: A parser crashed after writing chunks but before acknowledging. What happens on redelivery if chunk IDs are deterministic?
options: Repeated upserts, no duplicates
The queue stops for that item
Duplicate chunks appear
The document is lost
mcq.why: Idempotency makes at-least-once delivery safe.

interview.followUp: What happens without it during a big backfill?

mcq.q: Why are PDFs hard to extract text from?
options: They contain no text at all, only drawings
They are always encrypted and must be unlocked
They hold images only, so OCR is always needed
They place glyphs on pages, not text in reading order
mcq.why: Layout analysis is needed to recover reading order.

mcq.q: What does a scanned document need that a born-digital PDF does not?
options: A larger embedding model
Translation
No processing
OCR (image to text)
mcq.why: Scanned pages are images with no text layer.

mcq.q: Why record OCR confidence per page?
options: So low-confidence pages get review
To speed up the OCR engine
To reduce the storage used
To translate low-quality pages
mcq.why: Poor scans produce unreliable text.

mcq.q: How should tables be stored for retrieval?
options: Dropped from the index to avoid noise
Stored as images only, linked from text
As rows and columns, with the original kept
Flattened into one line of text per table
mcq.why: Flattening loses which number belongs to which column.
distractors: Images cannot be searched as text.

mcq.q: How should images and diagrams be indexed?
options: Caption them, OCR their text, link back
Embed only the image's file name
Convert each image into a table
Ignore them, as text matters most
mcq.why: Multimodal embeddings can also index images directly.

mcq.q: Why preserve headings, list numbering and page numbers as metadata?
options: PDF requires them as structured fields
They reduce the cost of indexing each page
They help chunking, filters and citations
They speed up the answer model's replies
mcq.why: For example, “Policy 4.2, page 17”.

mcq.q: Per-diem answers are wrong because a region-by-limit table was flattened to text. What fixes it?
options: Lower the model's temperature
Store the table as rows
Increase the chunk overlap
Use a bigger answer model
mcq.why: Row-as-sentence chunks keep each value with its row and column.

mcq.q: A parse produced a lot of text. Can you assume it was read correctly?
options: Only if the output is long
Yes, any text means success
Only if it found headings
No: run a quality gate first
mcq.why: Volume is not correctness.
distractors: Headings can come out while tables fail.

mcq.q: Which are signals a parse quality gate should check? Choose all that apply.
options: A high rate of non-dictionary words
Low OCR confidence
The file's author name
Almost no extracted text
mcq.why: Flag or reject such outputs for review.
distractors: Authorship says nothing about parse quality.

mcq.q: Why route scanned pages to a separate OCR pool?
options: To delete scanned pages later
Scanned pages need no parsing
OCR needs heavier, often GPU, capacity
OCR is faster than parsing
mcq.why: Separate pools keep heavy work from blocking normal parsing.

mcq.q: A pipeline's PDFs parse fine, but answers about one supplier's invoices are empty. The parser returns blank text for those files. What is the likely cause, and what helps?
options: They are scanned images with no text layer; route them to OCR
The answer model ignores invoices; switch to a larger one
The invoices are too long; split them into smaller chunks
The embedding model lacks invoice terms; fine-tune it first
mcq.why: Scans need OCR; the quality gate should flag near-empty pages.
distractors: The text never reaches the model.
Splitting empty text yields empty chunks.
There is no text to embed yet.

mcq.q: OCR on a 50-page scanned contract reports confidence below the 0.80 threshold on 6 pages. A reviewer takes 4 minutes per page. How much review time does this contract add?
options: 24 minutes, for the 6 low-confidence pages only
4 minutes, one review for the whole file
200 minutes, reviewing all 50 pages
176 minutes, for the 44 confident pages
mcq.why: Only flagged pages go to review: 6 × 4 = 24 minutes.
distractors: The point of the confidence score is to review only weak pages.

mcq.q: Where must access control be enforced in a RAG system?
options: In retrieval, before content reaches the prompt
In the system prompt, as a clear instruction
After the answer is generated, by a filter
In the user interface, by hiding sources
mcq.why: The model sees whatever is retrieved.
distractors: The model can be manipulated and has read the content.
The content has already reached the model.
Hiding output does not stop leaks.

mcq.q: What is early binding?
options: Giving every user access to every document
Checking each result with the source API after search
Asking the model which documents the user may see
Storing allowed principals per chunk and filtering inside search
mcq.why: Fast, but correctness depends on keeping ACLs in sync.

mcq.q: What is late binding?
options: Checking candidates with the source's permission API
Caching each user's results for a short time
Filtering by ACL metadata at index time
Deleting documents that some users cannot see
mcq.why: Always current, but slower; over-fetch to keep enough results.
distractors: Caching is not a permission check.

mcq.q: What is common practice for permissions?
options: Late binding only, checking every result on every query
Trust the system prompt to hide restricted content
No checks at all, since staff users are trusted
Early binding plus late checks for sensitive sources
mcq.why: Combine speed with currency.

mcq.q: Where should the tenant ID for a query come from?
options: The model's tool output
The server, from the session
The prompt template text
The user's chat message
mcq.why: Never from the prompt or model output (16.4).

mcq.q: An ACL for a document is unknown. What should retrieval do?
options: Treat it as deny
Ask the user
Treat it as allow
Ask the model
mcq.why: Fail closed.

mcq.q: Why keep an urgent deny list?
options: To cache answers for revoked users
To store passwords for later checks
To speed up search for most users
ACL sync lags; it blocks revocations at once
mcq.why: It is checked against the authoritative source on every query.

mcq.q: What must cache keys include so a revocation also invalidates cached answers?
options: Nothing beyond the query
Access scope and policy version
Only the question text
Only the request timestamp
mcq.why: Otherwise a cached answer keeps serving revoked content.
distractors: Revoked users would get cached answers.
Different users may see different answers.
Time alone does not reflect access.

mcq.q: The system prompt says “don't reveal restricted documents”. Is that access control?
options: Yes, if the model is told firmly
No: the model has already seen it
Only for small, simple models
Yes, if the prompt is long and clear
mcq.why: Enforce access before generation.
distractors: No model makes it access control.

mcq.q: A user loses access at minute 5; ACLs sync every 30 minutes; there is no deny list or late check. When does access really end?
options: At the next sync, up to 30 min later
Immediately, when access is removed
Never, until reindexing
After one hour, at the next full sync
mcq.why: The deny list or a late check closes that window.

mcq.q: A support agent is moved to another team at 10:00. ACLs sync every 30 minutes. At 10:05 the assistant still shows them a sensitive case from their old team. What prevents this?
options: A longer ACL sync interval so changes batch together
A system prompt telling the model not to show the old team's cases
Removing the case from the cache only
An urgent deny list checked on every query until the sync catches up
mcq.why: Index-level sync always lags; a deny list blocks revoked access at once.
distractors: The model has already received the case.

mcq.q: ACLs sync every 15 minutes, and permission-change events update the index within 1 minute but are missed about 2% of the time. With no deny list, what is the worst-case window for a missed revocation?
options: About 30 minutes, two sync cycles
Up to about 15 minutes, until the next periodic sync
About 1 minute, since events are fast
Zero, since events update the index directly
mcq.why: A missed event leaves the old ACL until the next full sync.
distractors: That holds only when the event arrives.

mcq.q: Why are vendor benchmarks a poor guide to production?
options: They test answers, not retrieval
They use too much data to be useful
Clean public data, no filters, no writes
They are always wrong on purpose
mcq.why: Your benchmark must reproduce your conditions.

mcq.q: How do selective permission filters affect ANN search?
options: They have no effect on ANN search
They always speed ANN search up
They remove the need for ANN
They can change latency and recall a lot
mcq.why: A user who sees 2% of the corpus behaves very differently.
distractors: Selective filters change behaviour a lot.
They can slow it or hurt recall.

mcq.q: Why run the benchmark while updates stream in?
options: Writes hurt latency and recall in practice
To make the benchmark finish faster
It is not needed for ANN indexes at all
To test the cache hit rate under load
mcq.why: Production indexes receive writes continuously.

mcq.q: Which measures should a retrieval benchmark report together?
options: Only ANN recall against exact search, nothing else
Recall (ANN and labels), latency percentiles at QPS, cost
Only the cost per million queries at peak
Only the average latency over the whole run
mcq.why: Trade-offs are only visible together.

mcq.q: Why benchmark at 10%, 30% and 100% of the target corpus?
options: To save money on the full run only
Because 100% cannot be loaded
Because the vendor requires it
To see the trend, not extrapolate
mcq.why: Behaviour changes with scale.
distractors: It can; it is just one point.

mcq.q: A benchmark repeats the same queries many times. What does it mostly measure?
options: The cache
Recall
Write throughput
Real retrieval latency
mcq.why: Use varied queries sampled from logs.
distractors: Cached results are faster than real ones.

mcq.q: In the topic's example, reaching 0.95 recall costs about 10 ms clean but about 25 ms with selective filters. What should you plan with?
options: Neither
The average of both
The clean number
The filtered number
mcq.why: Only the realistic condition predicts production.

mcq.q: The laptop ANN lab uses random vectors. How does that affect recall?
options: Recall cannot be measured at all
Recall is optimistic for real data
Pessimistic: random vectors lack clusters
It has no effect on recall
mcq.why: It still teaches the efSearch curve and memory behaviour.

mcq.q: Which cost figure should a retrieval benchmark report?
options: Cost per vector stored only
The vendor's list price
Nothing
Cost per million queries
mcq.why: It converts infrastructure into a comparable unit.

mcq.q: A team benchmarks on a 1% sample and extrapolates linearly to 100%. What is the risk?
options: The sample is too large to be fast
Memory and latency may not scale linearly
Recall always improves at scale
No risk; scaling is linear
mcq.why: Measure at several scale steps.
distractors: Memory and latency often are not.

mcq.q: When should you adopt an advanced retrieval technique?
options: Never; simple retrieval is always enough
Whenever a new technique is published
Always, for completeness of the stack
When evaluation shows a common failure it fixes best
mcq.why: Simpler fixes first: parsing, hybrid search, reranking, query rewriting.

mcq.q: What does hierarchical search do?
options: Indexes section and document summaries too, coarse first
Builds a knowledge graph of the entities in documents
Uses one vector per token of each chunk for matching
Routes each question between several retrieval tools
mcq.why: It helps big-picture questions over very large corpora.

mcq.q: How does late interaction (ColBERT) score a document?
options: A cross-encoder that reads each query–document pair
Per-token vectors; sum of each query token's best match
One vector per document, compared once with the query
BM25 computed over the document's subword tokens
mcq.why: Fine-grained matching that a single vector blurs.

mcq.q: A 2-token query: token 1's best document-token similarity is 0.9, token 2's is 0.6. What is the MaxSim score?
What is the main cost of late interaction?
options: It removes the need for reranking
It needs no storage at all
Many more vectors and special indexes
No cost beyond a normal index
mcq.why: Compression and indexes such as PLAID reduce it.

mcq.q: Which questions do knowledge graphs (GraphRAG) help with most?
options: Image search across documents
Multi-hop and corpus-wide questions
Single-fact lookup questions
Exact keyword lookups
mcq.why: Extraction is expensive and must be kept fresh.

mcq.q: What does agentic retrieval do?
options: An agent picks sources, rewrites, judges, iterates
Caches answers so repeated questions are cheap
Embeds new documents faster as they arrive
Removes the need for any search indexes
mcq.why: More LLM calls per question, higher latency and variance.

mcq.q: Only 6% of queries were multi-hop, and query decomposition fixed most of them. What should the team do about a knowledge graph?
options: Defer it
Replace all retrieval with it
Build it immediately
Remove decomposition
mcq.why: The evidence does not justify the cost.

mcq.q: A user asks “Which merchant category had the most fraud this month?”. What is the right tool?
options: A SQL query over structured data
HyDE over the fraud reports
A knowledge graph of merchants
Vector search over chunks
mcq.why: Aggregates need exact computation, not a few retrieved chunks.

mcq.q: A team adopts GraphRAG because it is popular. What is missing?
options: Nothing; popularity is enough
More documents in the corpus
A failure analysis showing the gap
A bigger GPU for extraction
mcq.why: Adopt by evidence, not by name.
